name: Jin Dynasty (Jurchen, 1115–1234)
summary: A dynasty founded by the Jurchen people. It destroyed the Liao, took north China from the Song in 1127, and was finally conquered by the Mongols in 1234.

location.value: From Outer Manchuria in the north to the Qinling–Huai river line in the south.

terrain.value: Manchurian forests, the north China plain and the Yellow River valley.
terrain.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

climate.value: Cold north, temperate plain; Yellow River floods.
climate.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

resources.value: North China’s farmland, horses from Manchuria, and iron.
resources.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

disasters.value: The Yellow River changed course in 1194, causing great floods.
disasters.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

urbanisation.value: Zhongdu (Beijing) became the capital in 1153; Kaifeng was taken from the Song.

disease.value: An epidemic struck besieged Kaifeng in 1232.
disease.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

migration.value: Jurchen military households moved into north China.
migration.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

economicBase.value: Farming in north China, plus tribute from the Southern Song.
economicBase.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

tradeRoutes.value: Border markets with the Song and trade with Xi Xia.
tradeRoutes.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

moneyAndTax.value: Chinese coins and paper money, which later suffered severe inflation.

inequality.value: The Jurchen Wanyan clan and military households over Chinese farmers.
inequality.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

governmentType.value: Monarchy that increasingly followed Chinese-style government.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

keyRulers.value: Aguda (Taizu, 1115–1123), Taizong, Wanyan Liang, Shizong (1161–1189), Aizong (1224–1234).

succession.value: Often violent: Wanyan Liang murdered his predecessor (1150) and was himself killed (1161).
succession.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

institutions.value: Chinese-style bureaucracy and exams; the Jurchen meng’an mouke military units.
institutions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

stability.value: Stable under Shizong; collapsed under Mongol attack from 1211.
stability.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

eliteConflict.value: Coups and defections during the Mongol wars.
eliteConflict.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

armyAndTech.value: Heavy cavalry; gunpowder weapons such as the “thunder crash bomb” used against the Mongols (1232).
armyAndTech.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Liao (1125) and the Northern Song capital Kaifeng (1127); a century of war with the Song; Mongol invasion from 1211.

territoryChange.value: About 4.75 million km² around 1186, ruling northern China and Manchuria.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Song, Western Xia and the Mongols.
alliancesRivals.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

inventions.value: Early gunpowder weapons, including fire lances.
inventions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

scienceEducation.value: A Jurchen script, civil service exams and schools.
scienceEducation.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

openness.value: Jin emperors gradually adopted Chinese customs; Confucianism revived.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and canals in northern China; horses for the army; paper money for trade.

religion.value: Buddhism, Taoism, Confucianism, folk religion; the Quanzhen school of Taoism began here.

languageWriting.value: Jurchen (with its own script, from 1119), Chinese and Khitan.
languageWriting.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

artsArchitecture.value: Zaju drama and the Lugou (Marco Polo) Bridge (1189–1192).
artsArchitecture.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

socialStructure.value: Jurchen military households, Chinese officials, farmers.
socialStructure.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

sharedIdentity.value: Jurchen identity, which later inspired the Manchus.
sharedIdentity.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

dailyLife.value: Chinese-style timber houses in towns; Jurchen villages with heated platforms (kang); millet, wheat and meat.

neighbours.value: The Song, Western Xia, Goryeo and the Mongols.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

ideasReligions.value: Quanzhen Daoism and Neo-Confucian learning spread in the north.
ideasReligions.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

colonisation.value: None overseas; many Jurchen settled in northern China as military households.
colonisation.source: Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

riseSignals.value: Aguda united the Jurchen tribes and founded the dynasty in 1115.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

peakPeriod.value: Under Shizong (1161–1189), a time of peace and prosperity.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

declineSignals.value: The Mongol invasion from 1211 and the loss of Zhongdu (Beijing) in 1215.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Jin dynasty (1115–1234) (checked 6 Nov 2026); Twitchett & Tietze, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)

outcome.value: Conquered by the Mongols in 1234 (fall of Caizhou).

sources.value: History of Jin. Checked against Wikipedia (“Jin dynasty (1115–1234)”).

overallCertainty.value: Good. Based on the official History of Jin.

knownFor.label: Thunder crash bomb
knownFor.note: An iron-cased gunpowder bomb used against the Mongols.

knownFor.label: Jurchen script
knownFor.note: A script made for the Jurchen language.
